query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: When exposed to high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions, the structural and chemical stability of multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by an interplay between high configurational entropy and controlled surface segregation. Specifically, a modest surface enrichment (even with low noble-metal content) forms a passivating layer that suppresses further atomic diffusion and phase separation, thereby preserving the nanoparticle’s homogeneous core.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles possessing a homogeneous bulk composition with minimal surface segregation.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled compositional modifications—introducing slight variations in the noble-metal or selected element content—and perform high-temperature in situ environmental TEM, in parallel with atomistic/mesoscale simulations, to monitor and predict surface segregation and degradation kinetics.
generation.conditions: High-temperature service regimes: catalytic conditions (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric conditions (473–1923 K) in inert or controlled reactive atmospheres; formulations deliberately designed with low noble-metal content.
generation.structural_mediator: A passivating surface layer formed by modest enrichment of specific elements (e.g., the low-noble-metal component) that reduces surface diffusion.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy inherent to the equiatomic nanoparticles retards bulk atomic diffusion and phase coarsening, while controlled surface segregation induces a passivating layer that further limits diffusion and prevents deleterious phase separation at the nanoparticle surface during high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that engineered to favor slight surface segregation will exhibit lower rates of coarsening and phase separation under high-temperature testing compared to uniformly composed nanoparticles. Measured outcomes will include a more stable morphology, slower grain boundary evolution, and maintained overall compositional homogeneity in the core.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with a strictly homogeneous distribution and no induced surface segregation, which are expected to show a higher susceptibility to diffusion-driven phase separation and coarsening under the same temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: Valid for multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles below a critical size (where diffusion lengths are comparable to particle size) and with low noble-metal content; effects may differ if external factors (e.g., support interactions or oxidative environments) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical compositional thresholds for beneficial surface segregation versus harmful phase separation, as well as the quantitative impact of environmental conditions (e.g., slight oxidation), remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near-equiatomic nanoparticles: one with a controlled slight enrichment of a selected low-noble-metal element to encourage formation of a passivating surface layer, and a control set with a uniform composition. Expose both sets to high-temperature conditions within the service regimes (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use) under identical atmospheric conditions. Use in situ environmental TEM paired with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to monitor surface composition changes and morphological evolution. Concurrently, run atomistic simulations to predict diffusion profiles and expected rates of surface passivation.
measurements: Nanoparticle morphology and grain size (high-resolution TEM)
Phase separation or coarsening indicators (TEM imaging, diffraction patterns)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles engineered for slight surface segregation do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in phase separation or coarsening compared to the baseline uniform nanoparticles—i.e., if there is no measurable formation of a passivating surface layer or if both sets show similar degradation kinetics—the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
